anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: Its approved L1 task requires rotating a 5×5×3 voxel pile, identifying exposed faces, ray-clicking the correct blocker, extracting four diamonds, and managing durability, lava, and support-collapse consequences. Pearl Lattice L1 is a 4×4×4 transparent board with one pre-authored planar line one pearl short; the input is a generic legal-column cycle followed by confirmation, with no ray targeting, hazard, collapse, or durability. Pearl Lattice L3 adds a two-route cross-depth fork and a rival response, but it still has substantially less motor precision than this approved L1.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: Gyroscopic Tilt Board L3 requires closed-loop control of a moving ball with momentum, friction, collision, ordered lamps, wells, and a settling cup; the approved full surface is an analog drag held over physics ticks, and its grader replays minimum ticks and control changes. Pearl Lattice L3 is turn-based: clicks change only the selected column or place a pearl, the rival responds after confirmation, and the automatic projection does not alter the selected column or expire a move. Pearl therefore has a legitimate 3D planning burden but a much lower continuous-control burden than this approved L3 anchor.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: Blind Dice Courier L4 spans an 18×11 warehouse with five barriers and face gates, requires a 48–105-roll route, and hides orientation except at the initial reveal and scanners. Every accepted roll changes both position and die orientation, so later gate decisions depend on a long hidden state trace. Pearl Lattice L4 exposes its board state, uses a 4×4×4 volume, and its raised fork still follows a short shared-defense/remaining-endpoint sequence. Pearl Lattice L4 is materially below this approved L4 in dependent path length and memory, while adding its own 3D support-reading burden.

Pearl Lattice L5 has a fixed visible initial board and a deterministic rival response, with the same short fork structure as lower Pearl levels, but raises 3D line interpretation, clutter, and preview ambiguity. Pearl Lattice L5 is below this approved L5 in changing-state planning and exact outcome constraints.

visible_baseline_solution: From screenshots alone, the agent must read the projected 4×4×4 lattice, distinguish player pearls from rival pearls, identify the rival's visible three-pearl threat and the two player routes that share the missing cell, and account for the lowest free y layer in the selected (x,z) column. At the baseline, the first useful placement is the shared defensive column. The clockwork rival then makes its visible authored response, blocking one of the player's immediate fork endpoints; the agent must reread the changed volume and choose the remaining endpoint. In Full mode, it repeatedly clicks the lattice surface to cycle the visible preview, uses the sidebar's coordinate/landing-layer readout, clicks the separate confirmation zone, and finally clicks CERTIFY WIN. The board projection keeps rotating, but the selected column remains actionable and no placement expires while the view turns. A wrong placement can end the attempt; the available recovery is to certify the failed state/abandon and receive a fresh lattice, not to undo a placement. Success requires a mode-valid cycle event, gravity-consistent player and rival placements, a player four-line with no rival line, and a completed certification.

baseline_judgment.rationale: The current L3 configuration is a plausible provisional mid-level Pearl Lattice task: it is above L1's one-line, one-placement planar problem because it adds a cross-depth fork and a state-changing rival response, and it is below Blind Dice Courier L4 and Exact-Change Candy Cascade L5 in dependent-state length, hidden memory, and changing-board planning. It is also below Gyroscopic Tilt Board L3 in continuous motor control, so the comparison is primarily spatial/planning rather than control difficulty. I would retain L3 for this baseline provisionally, but revise the ladder around it because L2 and L3 share the same geometry, prefill, opponent policy, and short response skeleton; L3's added clutter is real but its larger move ceiling is more forgiving.

concise_summary: Pearl Lattice's current L3 Full task is a plausible provisional 3D planning level and preserves its Full/Simplified world and replay contract. L1->L2, L3->L4, and L4->L5 have source-supported spatial changes, but L2->L3 is only weakly separated because its decision skeleton is unchanged and its move ceiling is looser. The profile ladder should be calibrated/revised before treating all five labels as equally spaced.
